doc.title: Kenny Davern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 16, 2001 [interview 2 of 2]

title: Jelly Roll Morton's 'Deep Creek' and what the blues means
summary: Davern chose Jelly Roll Morton records as a kid and praises 'Deep Creek' and other blues recordings.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Where the blues came from: Handy, Bolden and early blues

blocks.x: You seem to be really attracted to — oh gosh I don’t know if “authentic” is the right word, but a certain kind of historical thing. Like I know you are very fond of Jelly Roll.

Oh yeah. I had a choice when I was a kid when I first started to collect records, of buying a Count Basie album, which had “Every Tub” in it, Columbia ten inchers, three or four to the set, or the Jelly Roll Morton re-issues on Green Label Victor. Well the guys would play it, they were very nice in those stores then, they’d play me a band from each one. He’d advise me to take the Count Basie one, which is about the time it came out, I guess 1946, 47. No. at age 11 or 12 I instinctively went to the Jelly Roll Morton aisle. And I wore “Deep Creek” out until it turned white, until the green label, actually the whole record. Because that was to me one of the most profound blues recordings ever made. You know? Are you familiar with that?
Was that Leon Rapollo on that?
No, no, this was Jelly Roll Morton.
I know that, but who was—

Well it was one of his not very good later bands. Procope played, Paul Barnes played the soprano solo, Procope played the clarinet solo, but it was just the bass sustained and notes, regular twelve bar blues, the tuba played long tones. And after every chorus they upped it a fourth. And then another soloist would come. And Jelly Roll had it going so that it just kept moving, rhythmically, in the background, and then the solos brought it up. It was one of the very most profound records I ever heard in my life. In other words they did several things, “well how did you learn to play the blues?” Well you learn the blues by feeling the blues, one. But to play them, if you want to hear real blues, I mean it’s like listening to “Back to the Land” with Lester Young and King Cole and Buddy Rich. That trio record? There is a perfect example of the greatest blues playing of all time. This was

an example to me of great blues playing. “Deep Creek” with Jelly Roll Morton. Probably about 1930 when that record was made. Another example of great blues playing that influenced me was Pee Wee Russell playing “The Last Time I Saw Chicago,” with Joe Sullivan and Zutty Singleton. You want to learn the play the blues? You absorb those critters. You know. Maybe you’ll come up with something. Because if you can’t play a convincing blues, then you can’t play the music. Period. It doesn’t matter what color you are.
